segments.narration: Her blood knocked out 23 hospital workers in minutes. In February 1994, Gloria Ramirez was rushed into a California emergency room with severe heart complications. But as nurses drew her blood, the room suddenly smelled like ammonia and garlic.

Inside the syringe, strange white crystals floated in her dark blood. Seconds later, the nurse holding the needle collapsed. Another passed out cold, and a third lost control of her limbs as panic tore through the hospital.
Twenty-three staff members dropped with mysterious symptoms, forcing a total evacuation of the ER into the parking lot. Was this a biohazard leak, or was her body producing a deadly poison?
Scientists at Lawrence Livermore Laboratory finally cracked the puzzle. Ramirez had been applying a common pain relief cream called DMSO, which accumulated in her failing kidneys.
When paramedics pumped high-pressure oxygen into her system, it chemically transformed that harmless cream into dimethyl sulfate—a lethal chemical weapon inside her own veins.

verdicts.claim: In February 1994, 23 hospital workers suffered symptoms after exposure to Gloria Ramirez's blood.
verdicts.note: The reference article states that on February 19, 1994, twenty-three people in Ramirez's vicinity became ill after exposure to her body and blood.

verdicts.claim: Medical staff noticed an unusual ammonia smell and pale crystals in Ramirez's blood sample.
verdicts.note: The article confirms nurse Susan Kane smelled an ammonia-like odor from the blood tube, and medical resident Julie Gorchynski saw manila-colored (yellow-brown) crystallized particles in the blood.

verdicts.claim: The emergency room was evacuated due to staff falling ill.
verdicts.note: The article confirms staff was ordered to evacuate all emergency room patients to the parking lot outside after multiple staff members fainted.

verdicts.claim: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory investigated the Gloria Ramirez incident.
verdicts.note: The article notes that the Riverside Coroner's Office contacted Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to investigate the incident.

verdicts.claim: The leading theory concludes that oxygen therapy converted DMSO in Ramirez's system into toxic dimethyl sulfate.
verdicts.note: The article states that an investigation by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory theorized oxygen administered during transport converted self-administered DMSO in her system into toxic dimethyl sulfate.
